Jamie —

Thanks for the detail and the report. Short answer: we can support both models and will include explicit pricing and SLA language. High-level options below so you can tell me which direction you prefer before I draft the amendment.

Option A — Hard cap (Committed only)
- Reserved: additional 8 A100-equivalent GPUs added to your dedicated pool (isolated).
- Throughput: baseline guaranteed to the committed pool; no burst beyond the hard cap.
- Billing: flat monthly committed fee, no overage charges.
- Pros/Cons: Predictable spend, but you can experience request throttling during spikes unless you provision excess capacity.

Option B — Committed + On-demand spillover
- Reserved: additional 8 GPUs reserved as above.
- Burst: requests that exceed committed capacity can automatically spill to on-demand capacity (same region) at a premium token rate.
- Safety: configurable hard cap threshold and per-minute spill limits to control spend.
- Pros/Cons: smoother UX during bursts, cost variability during extreme peaks.

Operational notes:
- Throughput guarantees: we can include a baseline p99 token latency target for the committed pool and an SLO for end-to-end success rate. Spillover requests are best-effort and subject to availability — we will provide a documented fallback path (route to compatible quantized variant or lower-concurrency queue) when on-demand capacity is exhausted.
- Rollout: we recommend a two-week trial of committed + spillover to observe real burst patterns, then convert to a longer-term amendment.
- Timeline: we can provision the committed GPUs within 7–10 business days after the amendment is signed.

I've attached a draft amendment (renewal_draft_March23_v1.pdf) with line-item pricing for both options and a recommended mutual action plan (MAP). Can you review and let me know which option you prefer or if you'd like a blended plan (hard cap with occasional stamped spill credits)?

Best,
Rohan Mehta
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
